title: Private credit defined at last
full_text:
Private credit in Australia could soon get its first formal definition, just in time for the corporate regulator to narrow its focus on the secretive industry.
The Financial Services Council on Wednesday published its plan for the private credit sector, requiring its members to adhere to new disclosure, liquidity and valuation standards.
This comes as the market regulator published its updated corporate plan, laying out its priorities for the year ahead including a continued focus on private credit.
The Australian Securities & Investments Commission has said some lenders are putting their interests ahead of investors. ASIC has also been critical of the way private credit has been framed by some lenders.
But for the first time, the FSC has proposed a formal definition for the novel area of finance: “lending activities conducted through private market structures where debt instruments, loans, credit exposures or similar financing arrangements are not publicly traded”.
“For the avoidance of doubt, private credit may include privately negotiated lending, credit or financing exposures, including warehouse facilities and exposures to securitisation vehicles, where those exposures are not publicly traded or widely issued publicly,” the FSC said.
“Private credit does not include ordinary lending activities conducted by an authorised deposit-taking institution in its capacity as a balance-sheet lender outside a private markets fund.” FSC chief executive Blake Briggs told The Australian it was important to define what private credit was and wasn’t. “It will help discern good practice from poor practice,” he said.
But not all the major players in private credit are his members, like ASX-listed lender Metrics, for example.
Mr Briggs hoped the pressure of the FSC-aligned peers adopting its standards would go beyond the member cohort.
“We would be encouraging the Metrics of the world to apply this to their operations as well,” he said.
Among its recommendations, the FSC put forward proposed rules around how funds should value their loans and when they should shift those positions, being that each loan should be revalued quarterly. Breaches of loan covenants, restructuring of debt, deterioration of assets or increased risks would all trigger a revaluation.
Mr Briggs said increased transparency rules would also prevent lenders from flicking poor-performing loans out of funds to mask the actual performance of funds. “If there are still laggards within our membership, this will close that out,” he said.
Conflicts of interest should be identified, managed and disclosed. ASIC chair Sarah Court said the regulator was equally focused on addressing “unnecessary friction” for those trying to comply with its rules, “while making it harder for those causing harm to avoid scrutiny and accountability”.
ASIC’s gaze is equally on harm in the financial sector, including scams and debt collection, as well as new work on insurance, buy now, pay later, and superannuation advice fees.
The regulator will also look at how companies use AI.
In a reference to the scandal surrounding KPMG, ASIC also said it would focus on holding auditors and directors to account, as well as improving the standards of the audit sector. KPMG audit partners misused confidential client information to win work from their clients’ competitors and relied on a network of favours, conflicts and compromised independence to land lucrative tenders.
